To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Sindbis virus infection of neurons leads to cell death, and the mechanisms of cell death are different in different cell types.
Sindbis virus induces cell death by both apoptotic and non-apoptotic mechanisms, and that the mechanisms of neuronal cell death in brain and spinal cord are distinct.
Sindbis virus infection induces apoptosis in neurons of mice and that this cell death can be blocked by overexpression of Bcl-x(L) or by deletion of caspase 8.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of Sindbis virus pathogenesis, including the cellular pathways leading to neuronal cell death, as well as the cellular and molecular determinants that govern the outcome of infection.

understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying Sindbis virus-induced neuronal apoptosis, the age-dependent protection against neuronal apoptosis, and the cellular mechanisms that determine the outcome of infection (i.e. death versus persistent infection).
elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying the susceptibility of neurons to Sindbis virus-induced cell death.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Sindbis virus is a neurotropic virus, which infects neurons of all ages, but the outcome of infection is determined by a complex interplay between the virus and the cell.
Sindbis virus infections in neurons lead to cell death, but the nature of that death is dependent upon the age of the infected cell, the viral strain, and the cell type infected.
Sindbis virus infection induces cell death in some cells, but not others, and that the mechanisms that determine whether cell death will occur or not are not well understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Sindbis virus infection can cause apoptosis of neurons in the central nervous systems of newborn mice, but not of older mice.
Sindbis virus is an excellent model for studying the molecular mechanisms that govern neuronal apoptosis.
Sindbis virus infection of mammalian cells induces apoptosis in some but not in other cell types, depending on the cell type and the virus.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Sindbis virus infection is a valuable model to study the mechanisms that control neuronal cell death in the mammalian central nervous system.
Sindbis virus infections are a useful model for studying the molecular mechanisms that govern cell death in the brain and spinal cords.

Sindbis virus is an excellent model system to study cell death and survival pathways, and that the Sindbis virus-induced neuronal cell death model is an excellent model to study the mechanisms of neuroprotection.
